Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

issues.explanation: The Threat items describe a chronic interpersonal/home-intrusion danger template (monitoring for someone entering the home, planning escape routes, feeling unsafe specifically at night), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. These items imply fear of human attack rather than disaster-related threat.

Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure could occur after a disaster, but in combination with the highly interpersonal Threat items it reinforces a different trauma narrative than natural disaster. The Memory items are disaster-compatible, but the Threat cluster is not clinically coherent with that trauma context.

The threat items are centered on anticipating intentional human intrusion or attack (planning escape routes, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. Heightened alertness to loud sounds could fit disaster trauma, but these two more specific threat beliefs imply a different trauma context.

The appraisal 'The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down' is possible after a disaster, but in this profile it pulls toward a betrayal/response-failure formulation that is not supported elsewhere by the selected threat or memory items. Combined with the intrusion-focused threat items, it weakens coherence with a natural-disaster trauma profile.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat item about listening for someone entering the home implies an interpersonal/intrusion danger theme that is hard to reconcile with a primary trauma type of natural disaster. For a natural-disaster profile, loud sounds and generalized hypervigilance are plausible, but specifically monitoring for a person entering the home suggests a different trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: The appraisal that institutions failed to protect him is possible after a disaster, but in combination with the home-intrusion threat cue it contributes to a mixed interpersonal-threat profile rather than a coherent natural-disaster formulation. The rest of the profile centers on terror, overwhelm, and disorganized memory, so this item is questionable mainly because it pulls toward a different trauma narrative when paired with the flagged threat item.

vignette:
Peter has been a military medic for twenty years, a man who built his identity on the principles of order, control, and competence under pressure. Six months ago, that foundation was washed away in a flash flood that tore through the coastal town where he and his wife, Sarah, were stationed. The hurricane had been forecast, but no one predicted the storm surge that followed, collapsing the sea wall and turning streets into violent rivers. Peter was on duty, coordinating triage at a makeshift shelter in the town's community hall. He remembers the sound first-a low, grinding roar that was not the wind or the rain. It was the sound of the building's foundations giving way. The memory comes back not as a story but as a chaotic collage of sensory fragments. He can feel the floor lurching beneath his boots, see the panicked face of a young private he was treating, and hear the splintering crack of a support beam, but he cannot place these moments in a coherent sequence. He knows Sarah was at their home just a few blocks away, and in his mind, the image of their house being inundated is tangled with the chaos of the shelter collapsing.

In the months since, Peter has found that the world is no longer a safe place. He continues his duties on the base, but his body is in a constant state of high alert. The sudden thud of a helicopter landing on the nearby pad sends a jolt of pure adrenaline through him, his muscles tensing as if bracing for an impact. He has to consciously fight the urge to dive for cover. In the mess hall, he can no longer sit with his back to the door and finds himself scanning the room, his eyes tracking every movement, every unexpected noise. He knows, logically, that he is safe on a secure military base, but this knowledge provides no comfort. His body remains convinced that catastrophe is imminent. He hasn't had a full night's sleep in months; relaxation feels like a distant memory, a luxury his nervous system will no longer permit.

The man who prided himself on his steady hand and calm demeanor now feels like a stranger to himself. When he looks in the mirror, he doesn't recognize the haunted, exhausted man looking back. He was a husband; now he is a widower. He was a medic who saved lives; now he is the man who was organizing supplies while his own wife drowned. This thought circles endlessly, stripping his work of all its previous significance. What is the point of applying a tourniquet or dressing a wound when the universe is so fundamentally chaotic and cruel? His long-held belief in a just world, where skill and preparation could fend off the worst, has been utterly destroyed. He feels adrift, a man without a purpose or an identity.

When he is forced to recall the event during debriefings, the terror is as fresh and sharp as it was in the moment the lights flickered and the screaming began. The memory arrives with a suffocating wave of panic and grief that overwhelms him, forcing him to shut down, his mind going blank as a protective measure. To avoid this, he has systematically walled off his past. He threw out most of Sarah's belongings in a single, frantic afternoon because the sight of her photograph could trigger the cascade of fragmented images and the crushing weight of his failure. He no longer socializes with his unit, retreating to his sterile barracks room immediately after his shift ends. The isolation has become its own kind of prison. It was a near-miss during a training exercise last week that finally forced him into seeking help. A simulated explosion, part of the drill, sent him to the ground, and for a full minute, he was back in the collapsing hall, deaf to the instructor's commands. His commanding officer found him pale and shaking, and the referral became an order. Peter now sits in the waiting room, not with hope, but with the grim resignation of a man reporting his own internal casualties. He isn't sure if he can be fixed, but he is terrified of what will happen if he continues to shatter.
